Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 30
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Curriculum Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 33

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Family-Related Comments: Comments on family, Olfactory (Alcohol): Alcohol smell, Olfactory Danger Cue: Burnt smell
  Memory: Pain Recall: When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Injustice: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened

Vignette:
Kwame is a 30-year-old curriculum designer who came to therapy at the urging of his supervisor, who had noticed a steady decline in his focus and his increasing reluctance to attend team meetings. Kwame sat forward in his chair, his hands clasped tightly, and described the event that had upended his life eighteen months ago. He had been in a relationship with a man named Daniel for nearly two years, and what began as a partnership marked by occasional jealousy had escalated one night into a physical assault. Daniel had come home after drinking, and the smell of alcohol was thick on his breath. An argument over a missed phone call turned into Daniel grabbing Kwame by the collar, slamming him against the kitchen wall, and then striking him repeatedly across the ribs and face. Kwame remembered the sharp, acrid smell of something burning on the stove—a pan of oil Daniel had left on high heat—and the way that scent mixed with the alcohol and the metallic taste of blood in his mouth. He had managed to escape and call the police, but Daniel was never charged; the case was dropped due to insufficient evidence, and Kwame had moved to a new apartment alone.

In the months that followed, Kwame found that his body would not let him forget. When a memory of that night surfaced—often without warning—he would feel a searing pain in his ribs and jaw, exactly where Daniel’s fists had landed. The terror he had felt in that moment would return fully, as though he were pinned against the wall again. And sometimes, without any obvious cue, he would catch a whiff of burnt oil or alcohol, and his stomach would lurch. He had come to believe that the person he was now was a stranger. He used to be someone who laughed easily, who hosted dinner parties, who felt confident in his own skin. Now he felt fundamentally altered, as though the assault had stained something inside him. He often described feeling dirty, contaminated by what had happened, and he showered twice a day, sometimes scrubbing his skin until it was raw, though he knew logically that no amount of soap could wash away the memory.

The injustice of the dropped case gnawed at him. He would lie awake at night replaying the conversation with the detective, rehearsing what he should have said differently, certain that the system had failed him and that nothing had been done to hold Daniel accountable. This sense of unfairness made him hypervigilant in ways that affected his work. As a curriculum designer, he spent most of his day in an open-plan office, and he had begun to avoid the break room entirely because a colleague often heated up leftovers that smelled faintly of burnt food. He also found himself flinching whenever a coworker made an offhand comment about family—someone mentioning a sibling’s visit or a parent’s birthday—because those words now felt loaded with the threat of betrayal and violence. He had started eating lunch at his desk, alone, and he declined all invitations to after-work drinks, because the smell of alcohol on someone’s breath, even from across a bar, sent him into a cold sweat.

His avoidance had narrowed his world. He stopped dating entirely, believing that he could not trust his own judgment in relationships. He had stopped visiting his own mother, who lived two hours away, because the drive took him past the old apartment building. The consequence was a growing isolation that his supervisor had noticed, and Kwame had finally agreed to seek help because he was terrified that he would lose his job. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the feeling that he was dissolving into someone he did not recognize, and that no amount of scrubbing or avoiding would ever bring the old Kwame back. He hoped, though he could barely say it aloud, that therapy might help him feel clean again.
